title: Sarah Rogers: Free Speech, AI Diplomacy, and What America Owes Its Allies

reader_summary.headline: Sarah Rogers argues the US must protect free speech online and support its allies against restrictive foreign rules.
reader_summary.overview: Sarah Rogers explains that the US wants to spread AI tools that follow free speech rules rather than government control. She warns that European laws against insulting politicians could harm American internet companies and threaten allies. Rogers urges clear, neutral regulations that protect free speech while allowing users to filter harmful content.

key_points.text: The US wants to spread AI that follows free speech rules instead of government control.
key_points.evidence_quote: the proliferation of a Western AI stack is really a top priority for our entire administration. It should be a top priority for anyone who cares about freedom.

key_points.text: Sarah Rogers warns that letting Trump speak on X could trigger EU fines, linking speech rules to unrelated investigations.
key_points.evidence_quote: if you let president Trump speak, that is going to increase your exposure to adverse findings of liability in this other regulatory crackdown.

key_points.text: She argues European laws against insulting politicians or blasphemy should not apply globally to American internet companies.
key_points.evidence_quote: these European censorship laws, laws that make it illegal to insult a politician as it is in Germany, for example, or illegal to blaspheme Islam as some prosecutors argued recently in the UK, when you transpose those to a transnational internet

key_points.text: Rogers urges the US government to avoid arbitrary regulations and instead create clear, neutral rules that protect free speech.
key_points.evidence_quote: we should have a regulatory environment that's like crisp and principled words always clear what you have to do and what you can do to comply with the law.

key_points.text: The US government must protect American political freedoms and not threaten allies like French platforms hosting interviews with their leaders.
key_points.evidence_quote: if the US government, to go back to that Terry Breton letter, if the US government threatened Le Monde or threatened of a Vendee, these are French, French platforms for hosting an interview with Emmanuel Macron, the French government wouldn't stand for it. And we shouldn't stand for it.

notes: Katherine Boyle speaks with Sarah Rogers, Under Secretary for Public Diplomacy, about the intersection of AI, free speech, and global information systems. They discuss how major technological shifts, from the printing press to the internet to AI, have reshaped communication and power, and why this moment may be even more consequential. Recorded at the a16z American Dynamism Summit, the conversation explores the role of public diplomacy in the digital age, the risks of censorship and overregulation, and how governments are approaching AI as both a national security priority and a platform for global influence. Rogers also highlights the importance of maintaining “AI with a Western soul,” and why preserving open systems and freedom of expression will shape the future of innovation. thesis: Sarah Rogers argues that the proliferation of a Western AI stack that prioritizes individual reasoning, user consent, and rule-based principles is the United States' most important soft power tool. She contends that while previous administrations engaged in censorship and content removal to combat disinformation, her office now pursues transparency, truth, and reconciliation to make freedom of expression a primary prong of public diplomacy.
